title: EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook (December 2026) — the last edition before the 2026-12-11 funding cliff
source: EST: eia.gov/outlooks/steo/release_schedule.php, fetched direct 2026-09-08 (HTTP 200), lists "12/08/2026" for the December 2026 edition. The date reproduces independently from the same page's stated rule ("the first Tuesday following the first Thursday of each month", with a Federal holiday on the preceding Monday pushing the release to Wednesday): 2026-12-03 is a Thursday, the following Tuesday is 12-08, and 12-07 is not a Federal holiday, so no adjustment applies. Release window is stated on the same page as 12:00-12:15 pm ET. Filed estimate on two counts, neither of them date doubt: this calendar defines no `confirmed` prefix for the EIA (the standing schema gap eia-steo-2026-09-09 named), and this lane never self-confirms an event it discovered in-sweep
notes: Discovered during eia-steo-2026-10-06's never-assessed initial research (2026-09-08), off the same EIA release-schedule primary that dates the October edition. Proposed for two dated reasons beyond calendar completeness. FIRST, it is the one 2026 EIA publication with live appropriations risk: H.R. 6500 (PL 119-103, signed 2026-09-02) funds agencies only through 2026-12-11 per its section 106, so 12-08 sits three days inside the funded window with the cliff immediately behind it — and cr-expiry-2026-12-11 explicitly declines to inherit government-funding-deadline-2026-09-30's aversion base case, which makes a December STEO delay a real branch rather than a hypothetical one. The mitigating precedent is on the record and should be carried with the risk, not instead of it: EIA published the October 2025 STEO on 2025-10-07, seven days into the October 2025 lapse, and its announcement page carries the standing language that publications continue on established schedules. SECOND, eia-steo-2026-09-09's kill switch #4 names this edition alongside 2026-10-06 as the scoreboard for whether national 2027 electricity consumption is cut below 4,391 bkWh on data-center pauses spreading beyond Texas — the demand-side leg of docs/research/ai-energy-constraint.md, and a book-level input rather than an energy-sector footnote. Filed `low` on the sibling entries' reasoning: a forecast publication sets no policy and moves no equity tape.
